system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2149-09-20 14:46:00 to 2149-09-26 20:19:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

focal lesions.  There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilatation.
The common duct measures 4 mm.  The portal vein is patent with anterograde
flow.  There is no ascites.  The gallbladder is unremarkable, with no
gallstones, wall thickening, or pericholecystic fluid.  There is no
sonographic ___ sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having this abdominal pain again—same kind as my old pancreatitis episodes. It started about a week ago with nausea, then the pain came back in the middle and right side, going through to my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was it as severe as your last pancreatitis episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not quite as bad, but still pretty uncomfortable. I had a CT scan six days ago—my doctor said there might be some inflammation in the tail of my pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I reviewed that. It showed a slightly bulky tail but no clear signs of active pancreatitis. We’ll need to look deeper. You mentioned you left the hospital yesterday after getting orange juice and vomiting—why did you come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wasn’t getting better. The nausea kept coming back, and I felt weak. I knew I needed more help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now, give you IV fluids, and control your pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. Once your symptoms settle, we’ll try clear liquids. It might take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve also been feeling a bit feverish—temperature up to 100.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Your urine test showed some signs of infection—moderate bacteria and white cells—so we started you on Levaquin for a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had UTIs before. I’ve also been having trouble emptying my bladder sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be contributing. We’ll treat the infection and monitor. We also checked your blood work—your hemoglobin has been dropping a bit, so we’re watching for anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had iron deficiency before. Is that related to the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Given your history of malabsorption and Sjogren’s, we’re concerned there might be an issue in your small intestine. We’re planning an EGD and capsule endoscopy to look inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a capsule endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You swallow a small pill-sized camera that takes pictures as it moves through your gut. It helps us see the small bowel, which we can’t reach with regular scopes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds interesting. When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Early next week. First, we need you stable and hydrated. We also did an ultrasound today to check your gallbladder—everything looked normal, so it’s not gallstones causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. My mom had her gallbladder out—always worried I’d get it too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Nausea is less, but I still have some pain in the upper right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your kidney function is good, and your amylase and lipase are normal—so no active pancreatitis. But your potassium is a bit low at 3.1, so we’re giving you some supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had low potassium before—especially when I was on full-dose Florinef. I’m on half now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we kept it at half-dose because of that. Your blood pressure has been on the lower side—around 95 systolic—so we held your Betaxolol for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t felt dizzy, but I know I’d get more tachycardic if I stood up for long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I’m tired of just IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with clear liquids yesterday. Today, we’re giving you toast. How’s your stomach holding up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had the whole piece and no vomiting. Pain is still there but milder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re switching your pain meds from IV to oral Dilaudid. You can take it every few hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’d rather not be on IVs anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we did your EGD and capsule endoscopy. The upper endoscopy didn’t show anything obvious, but we took biopsies from your duodenum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did they find?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsies show chronic duodenitis—ongoing inflammation. It could be from celiac disease, Crohn’s, or another form of IBD. We’re sending more tests to figure it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a sigmoidoscopy years ago that showed inflammation. Could this be Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. That’s why we tried to do a colonoscopy—to look at the rest of your colon. But even after your prep, there was still too much stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I cleared out. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to come back and do a two-day GoLytely prep to clean things out fully. Then we can get a clear view.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’ve been on solids, no vomiting, pain is much better. We’re thinking about discharge in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue advancing your diet slowly. Stay on the omeprazole we started—it helps with gut inflammation. And take the Creon with meals; it helps with digestion since you have malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken Creon before. How long should I stay on it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, indefinitely. We’ll reassess once we get all your biopsy results and complete the colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your UTI treatment is complete—three days of Levaquin. No more fevers, and your symptoms have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. My bladder feels normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re clearing you for discharge today. You’re tolerating food, pain is minimal, and you don’t need IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to schedule the colonoscopy with a full prep. We’re also adding Midodrine for your orthostatic symptoms, and we lowered your Betaxolol dose to 10mg to keep your heart rate stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue amitriptyline for sleep, Lexapro for mood, and Florinef at 0.2mg twice daily. Take the hydromorphone only if pain flares up, and don’t hesitate to come back if you can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m glad I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for recurrent abdominal pain similar to prior pancreatitis episodes, but with normal lipase levels and only mild CT findings. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and pain control, then gradually advanced to a solid diet. A UTI was treated with a 3-day course of levofloxacin. EGD and capsule endoscopy revealed chronic duodenitis, suggesting possible small bowel disease or IBD, though the etiology remained unclear. A colonoscopy was attempted but unsuccessful due to inadequate bowel prep, requiring a future repeat with full GoLytely preparation. Her orthostatic hypotension was managed with dose adjustments to fludrocortisone and betaxolol, and she was discharged home in good condition, tolerating oral intake and requiring no IV medications.
